relationship: Moses' death followed by Joshua's succession
rationale: Joshua's opening after Moses' death follows the conclusion recording that death and Joshua's reception of understanding and Israel's obedience; the two records retain their different introductory details.

relationship: Joshua son of Nun as Moses' attendant
rationale: Both explicitly identify Joshua son of Nun as Moses' attendant; Exodus describes his remaining at the tent, while Joshua opens with the Lord addressing him after Moses' death.

relationship: Promised leadership into possession and the command to cross
rationale: Moses announces Joshua going before Israel into possession; the later divine charge directs Joshua and the people to cross Jordan into the land being given them.

relationship: Repeated footsole-and-land promise
rationale: Both promise possession of the places trodden by the soles of Israel's feet; Joshua's charge expressly relates the gift to what was spoken to Moses.

relationship: Corresponding territorial boundary declarations
rationale: Both name wilderness, Anti-Lebanon, the Euphrates and the western or sunset sea as boundaries, preserving the source's actual geographical expressions without modern boundary verification.

relationship: Non-abandonment assurance to Joshua
rationale: Moses assures Joshua that the Lord will not fail or forsake him; the later divine speech similarly promises not to forsake or disregard him, distinguishing the speakers.

relationship: Joshua's courage and allotment of the sworn land
rationale: Both address Joshua with strength and courage because he will lead Israel into the land sworn to the fathers and give it as inheritance.

relationship: Obedience without turning right or left
rationale: Both command fidelity to the delivered commands without turning right or left; Joshua's personal charge also stresses strength and understanding, while Deuteronomy addresses Israel's life in the land.

relationship: Day-and-night meditation on the law and resulting prosperity
rationale: Both join meditation on the Lord's law day and night with prospering conduct; the psalm uses a fruitful tree image, while Joshua's charge stresses doing everything written.

relationship: Written law kept continually by a leader
rationale: Joshua must keep the law in his mouth and meditate continually; the royal instruction likewise requires retaining and reading a law scroll, preserving the distinct offices and descriptions.

relationship: Courage grounded in the Lord's presence
rationale: Both forbid fear and faintheartedness and call for strength and courage because the Lord is present; Deuteronomy addresses Israel collectively, while Joshua receives the later personal charge.

relationship: Same-chapter command introduction and actual instructions
rationale: Joshua's command to the scribes is followed by their specified task of passing through the camp, directing provision preparation and announcing the coming Jordan crossing.

relationship: Three-day preparation and the later camp instruction
rationale: The scribes are to announce crossing in three days; the later account has scribes passing through the camp after three days and directing departure behind the ark, without imposing an additional chronology.

relationship: Named eastern recipients of Moses' land grant
rationale: Joshua addresses Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh; Numbers explicitly names those same recipients in Moses' grant of the kingdoms of Sihon and Og.

relationship: Remembered Mosaic gift of the eastern possession
rationale: Joshua calls the eastern tribes to remember Moses' word that God gave them land; Deuteronomy records Moses declaring that divine gift while requiring armed service.

relationship: Eastern households remain while equipped men cross
rationale: Both distinguish wives, children and livestock remaining in the given towns from able men crossing armed before their brothers, retaining the particular household and military arrangement.

relationship: Return to the eastern inheritance after the brothers receive rest
rationale: Both condition the eastern men's return upon their brothers receiving rest and inheritance, explicitly retaining the land given by Moses as their eventual destination.

relationship: Same-chapter answer and the named addressees
rationale: The promise to do and go as Joshua commands answers his address to Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh; the response is not silently attributed to every Israelite.

relationship: Promised obedience and the preceding succession notice
rationale: The eastern tribes promise obedience to Joshua as to Moses and ask divine presence; the preceding book records Israel heeding Joshua after Moses laid hands on him.

relationship: Same-chapter renewed strength-and-courage exhortation
rationale: The tribes conclude their response by urging strength and courage, repeating the particular exhortation already spoken to Joshua by the Lord, while adding their own disobedience judgment.

relationship: Distinct scouting missions into the land
rationale: Both describe scouts examining the land and its cities; Deuteronomy's earlier mission uses twelve tribal men, while Joshua sends two young men specifically toward Jericho.

relationship: Rahab's reception of spies recalled in a faith example
rationale: Joshua records the spies lodging with Rahab; Hebrews explicitly names Rahab receiving the spies in peace and surviving, giving its own stated faith interpretation.

relationship: Same-chapter spying mission and the king's report
rationale: The report to Jericho's king identifies Israelite men entering to spy, corresponding to Joshua's stated commission and the two men's entry and lodging.

relationship: Same-chapter reported threat and royal demand
rationale: The king's demand that Rahab produce the men follows the report of Israelite spies entering Jericho, preserving the reason supplied for his command.

relationship: Same-chapter concealment and its specific location
rationale: The notice that the woman hid the men is developed by the roof and piled flax-stalk description, distinguished from the statements she makes to the messengers.

relationship: Same-chapter reported departure contrasted with actual concealment
rationale: Rahab tells the messengers the men left at gate closing; the narrative separately says she had hidden them on the roof, preserving the difference between her claim and narrated action.

relationship: Concealment explicitly recalled as the reason for preservation
rationale: Joshua2 describes Rahab hiding the spies among roof flax; Joshua6 explicitly says she and her paternal household were kept alive because she hid the spies.

relationship: Same-chapter pursuit route and the proposed hiding direction
rationale: The pursuers take the Jordan-crossing road; Rahab directs the young men to hide in the hill country until pursuit ends, preserving the specific contrasting routes without a modern map identification.

relationship: Same-chapter roof approach and Rahab's ensuing testimony
rationale: Rahab approaches the young men on the roof before sleep and then states her knowledge of the land gift, fear, Egyptian deliverance and the defeated kings.

relationship: Promised dread and Rahab's reported fear
rationale: The promise that dread of Israel would fall upon the land corresponds to Rahab's statement that fear of Israel has fallen upon her people, retaining her testimony's reported character.

relationship: Rahab's Red Sea report and the narrated dry crossing
rationale: Rahab recalls the Lord drying the Red Sea before Israel; Exodus narrates the sea made dry and Israel crossing, while also recording the Egyptian pursuit and destruction.

relationship: Rahab's report of Sihon and the conquest account
rationale: Rahab names the destruction of Sihon beyond Jordan among the deeds heard in Jericho; Numbers narrates his refusal of passage, defeat and Israel's occupation of his towns.

relationship: Rahab's report of Og and the Bashan encounter
rationale: Rahab names Og alongside Sihon as a defeated eastern king; Numbers narrates Og's battle at Edrei, the Lord's assurance and the defeat of him and his people.

relationship: Confession of the Lord as God in heaven and earth
rationale: Both expressly identify the Lord as God in heaven above and earth below; Rahab joins that confession with the fear produced by reported deeds, while Moses commands Israel to acknowledge it.

relationship: Requested household mercy and later preservation
rationale: Rahab asks mercy for her father's house in return for her mercy; the later narrative expressly records her and her entire paternal household remaining alive.

relationship: Named family rescue requested and narrated
rationale: Rahab asks rescue for her father, mother, brothers and household; the later account names those relatives among the people brought from her house by the spies.

relationship: Life guarantee and the ordered household rescue
rationale: The men pledge their lives, and Rahab asks mercy and faithfulness upon the city's delivery; Joshua later directs those spies to bring her and her belongings out, and they do so.

relationship: Same-chapter lowering window recalled in the sign instruction
rationale: The brief account says Rahab lowered the men through the window; their subsequent instruction identifies that same window for the scarlet-cord sign, without adding a missing house-wall description.

relationship: Same-chapter three-day hiding instruction and execution
rationale: Rahab directs hiding in the hill country for three days until the pursuers return; the men later remain there three days while the search fails.

relationship: Same-chapter oath-release declaration and following conditions
rationale: The declaration of freedom from the oath is followed by scarlet-window and household arrangements and the disclosure condition; the actual formulations are retained without recasting the oath as already canceled.

relationship: Household gathering instruction and the later removal
rationale: The men require Rahab's father, mother, brothers and paternal house to gather in her house; the later rescue names those relatives and all her kin being brought out.

relationship: Household-door boundary in distinct protective arrangements
rationale: The spies distinguish people protected inside Rahab's house from those leaving it; Exodus similarly forbids leaving the marked house before morning, with a different sign, danger and protecting action.

relationship: Same-chapter disclosure condition and the stated oath release
rationale: The men repeat freedom from the oath if anyone wrongs them or makes their words known, qualifying the earlier oath-release declaration without replacing anyone with an unstated single actor.

relationship: Rahab's sending of the messengers recalled by James
rationale: Joshua records Rahab agreeing and sending the men away, within the hill-country plan; James specifically recalls her reception and sending by another way, giving its works interpretation.

relationship: Same-chapter hill-country hiding follows the specified plan
rationale: The three-day stay in the hill country and unsuccessful pursuit enact Rahab's particular hiding direction, without adding an undisclosed encounter or escape route.

relationship: Same-chapter returned scouts report to their sender
rationale: The two young men return to Joshua son of Nun and relate their experiences, completing the mission introduced by his sending two young men to inspect Jericho.

relationship: Same-chapter scouts' report and the testimony they heard
rationale: The scouts report the Lord's land gift and the inhabitants' fear, corresponding to Rahab's statements about that gift and fear; the report is not treated as an independent census of every inhabitant.

relationship: Shittim as Israel's earlier lodging place
rationale: Joshua's party departs from Shittim for Jordan; Numbers explicitly records Israel lodging at Shittim, while describing a different episode there rather than the crossing itself.

relationship: Three-day camp preparation linked across the crossing account
rationale: The scribes' passage through camp after three days corresponds to the earlier scribal announcement of crossing in three days, without identifying an unprovided exact start time for both intervals.

relationship: Priests of Levi identified as ark bearers
rationale: The crossing instructions identify priests and Levites carrying the covenant ark; Moses' law-book handover likewise identifies priests who are Levi's sons and bear that ark.

relationship: Same-chapter following the ark with specified distance
rationale: The two-thousand-cubit separation qualifies the preceding instruction to follow the ark; the stated purpose is knowing the unfamiliar way, without importing a different reason for that distance.

relationship: Purification before an announced divine manifestation
rationale: Joshua requires purification before tomorrow's wonders; Exodus similarly requires purification before the Lord's announced Sinai descent, preserving its different third-day timing and garment instruction.

relationship: Same-chapter priests' ark-bearing command and narrated advance
rationale: Joshua commands priests to lift the ark and precede the people; the crossing departure later describes the priests lifting it ahead of the people.

relationship: Promised exaltation of Joshua and reported result
rationale: The Lord promises to exalt Joshua before Israel as one accompanied like Moses; the later account explicitly says the Lord exalted him and Israel feared him as Moses.

relationship: Same-chapter Jordan-standing command and narrated action
rationale: The command directs the ark-bearing priests into Jordan to stand; the account later describes their feet entering and their standing on dry ground while Israel crosses.

relationship: Same-chapter invitation to hear and the specified word
rationale: Joshua's invitation to hear the Lord's word introduces the declaration of divine presence, removal of the named nations, ark crossing and the predicted stopping water.

relationship: Corresponding seven nations and promised removal
rationale: Both name Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites, Amorites, Girgashites and Jebusites as nations removed before Israel; the list order and accompanying commands remain distinct.

relationship: Same-chapter ark crossing and the predicted water response
rationale: The announcement that the Lord-of-all-earth covenant ark crosses Jordan is developed by the prediction that its bearers' resting feet coincide with the failing and standing waters.

relationship: One representative per tribe for the stone undertaking
rationale: The command to choose twelve men, one per tribe, corresponds to the later command and summons of tribal representatives to carry the twelve river stones.

relationship: Same-chapter feet-and-water prediction and reported fulfillment
rationale: The priests' feet in Jordan are announced as the occasion of the water's stopping; the subsequent account describes their entry, the standing mass and the completed dry crossing.

relationship: Same-chapter ark preceding the people as commanded
rationale: The departure account places the priests' lifted covenant ark ahead of the people, matching Joshua's earlier direction that they lift it and go before the people.

relationship: Priests' feet entering and leaving with different water responses
rationale: The priests' feet enter the river at the beginning of the stopped-water crossing; when their feet later reach land, the water returns to its prior course and bank.

relationship: Stopped Jordan water recalled with an explicit Red Sea comparison
rationale: The narrative describes Jordan's waters standing and failing; the later explanation attributes their drying to the Lord and expressly compares it with the Red Sea, without replacing Kiriath-jearim's actual name.

relationship: Israel crossing a water barrier on dry ground
rationale: Both explicitly describe Israel crossing through the water's midst on dry ground; Exodus adds the water walls, while Joshua describes priests standing with the ark.

relationship: Completed crossing repeated as the next instruction's setting
rationale: The notice that the whole people finished crossing resumes the preceding description of priests standing on dry ground until all Israel completed its passage.

relationship: Repeated tribal representative requirement
rationale: Both require men from the sons of Israel with one from each tribe; the earlier instruction explicitly gives twelve, developed here by the following twelve-stone command.

relationship: Same-chapter twelve-stone transport command and execution
rationale: The instruction to carry twelve river stones to the night's camp is followed by the report that Israel took twelve stones, carried them over and set them in camp.

relationship: Summoned twelve men and the earlier selection command
rationale: Joshua summons twelve distinguished men, one per tribe, corresponding to the earlier instruction to choose twelve representatives rather than introducing a different tribal census.

relationship: Same-chapter individual stone-bearing charge and completed transport
rationale: Each tribal representative must carry a stone upon his shoulders; the later report records twelve stones taken from the river and carried into camp as directed.

relationship: Children's ritual question and a deliverance explanation
rationale: Both anticipate children asking the meaning of a visible observance or memorial and instruct parents to explain the Lord's deliverance, distinguishing the stones from the Passover service.

relationship: Stone explanation refers to the narrated ark-and-water crossing
rationale: The children's explanation says Jordan failed before the covenant ark; the earlier narrative supplies the announced stopping water, priests' entry and dry passage underlying that memorial.

relationship: Same-chapter completed stone transport answers the command
rationale: The people take twelve stones from Jordan and set them in camp, expressly acting as the Lord commanded Joshua in the earlier transport instruction.

relationship: Same-chapter distinct stone sets in Jordan and at Gilgal
rationale: Joshua sets another twelve stones under the priests' river-standing place, while the transported twelve are later erected at Gilgal; the two stated locations are not collapsed into one set.

relationship: Priests remain in the river until the people complete passage
rationale: Both keep the ark-bearing priests standing in Jordan during Israel's crossing; chapter4 additionally names completion of Joshua's instructions and the people's hurried passage.

relationship: Same-chapter completed human passage followed by the ark's crossing
rationale: The priests' standing until the people's passage is followed by the ark crossing after that completion; this unit's statement about stones before them is preserved without replacing it with another group.

relationship: Eastern tribes cross equipped according to the earlier arrangement
rationale: The named Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh cross equipped before Israel, corresponding to Joshua's earlier instruction to those tribes to leave households and send equipped men before their brothers.

relationship: Equipped crossing before the Lord for war
rationale: The forty thousand cross equipped before the Lord for battle; Numbers records the eastern men's promise of armed formation before the Lord, without importing this later number into their pledge.

relationship: Reported exaltation fulfills the announced comparison with Moses
rationale: The Lord exalts Joshua and Israel fears him as Moses, corresponding to the earlier promise that Israel would know the Lord accompanied Joshua as He accompanied Moses.

relationship: Same-chapter divine speech introduction and priests' exit command
rationale: The notice that the Lord spoke introduces the particular instruction for Joshua to command the ark-bearing priests out of Jordan, rather than an unspecified new oracle.

relationship: Same-chapter commanded message and Joshua's delivery
rationale: The Lord directs Joshua to command the priests out of Jordan; the next unit records Joshua giving those priests that precise exit command.

relationship: Same-chapter priests' exit command and resulting river restoration
rationale: Joshua orders the priests out; they then leave Jordan, set their feet on land and the water returns, supplying the narrated action following his command.

relationship: Priests' entry and exit frame the altered water flow
rationale: At entry the priests' feet meet overflowing water and the upstream mass stands; at exit their feet reach land and Jordan's water returns, preserving the two opposite transitions.

relationship: Arrival date and subsequent Passover observance
rationale: The people leave Jordan and camp at Gilgal on the first month's tenth day; the following chapter reports Passover on the fourteenth day, preserving the separate arrival and festival events.

relationship: Same-chapter camp stones receive the specific Gilgal location
rationale: Joshua sets at Gilgal the twelve stones taken from Jordan; the preceding transport account had already described carrying those stones over and setting them in camp.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated future children's stone question
rationale: Both anticipate sons asking what these stones mean; the repeated question frames the subsequent explanation of Israel's dry crossing and the Lord's power.

relationship: Children's crossing explanation and the original narrative
rationale: The words parents must tell their sons identify Israel's dry-ground Jordan crossing, matching the narrative that all the sons of Israel crossed on dry ground.

relationship: Explicit Red Sea comparison anchored in the earlier narrative
rationale: The Jordan explanation expressly compares its drying with the Red Sea; Exodus records the Lord making the sea dry and Israel entering on dry ground.

relationship: Divine power witnessed and resulting reverence
rationale: The memorial's purpose includes knowing the Lord's mighty power and revering Him; the sea account records Israel seeing His great hand, fearing Him and trusting God and Moses.

relationship: Reported deliverances produce fear among the land's inhabitants
rationale: The kings hear Jordan was dried and lose confidence; Rahab earlier describes fear after hearing the Red Sea and eastern-king reports, preserving the different hearers and events.

relationship: Circumcision command and the earlier covenant sign
rationale: Joshua is commanded to circumcise Israel using stone knives; Genesis commands circumcision as the covenant sign, with its own eighth-day and household stipulations rather than this particular camp procedure.

relationship: Stone used for circumcision in distinct episodes
rationale: Joshua makes sharp stone knives and circumcises Israel; Exodus likewise explicitly describes Zipporah taking a stone to circumcise her son, preserving the different agents and recipients.

relationship: Same-chapter circumcision populations stated in their actual forms
rationale: The explanatory introduction includes those born along the way and uncircumcised people from Egypt; the later notice identifies appointed sons circumcised by Joshua, without replacing either description with another edition's formulation.

relationship: Same-chapter completed action and its stated recipients
rationale: The brief statement that Joshua circumcised all these refers back to the immediately described uncircumcised groups, retaining the antecedent supplied by this edition.

relationship: Excluded wilderness generation with different stated durations
rationale: Both connect the disobedient wilderness generation with not seeing the sworn land; Joshua says forty-two years and adds its circumcision description, whereas Numbers states forty years tied to the scouting days.

relationship: Replacement generation and the land-entry promise to children
rationale: Joshua describes sons appointed in the earlier generation's place; Moses' land-entry declaration likewise promises the land to young children, preserving the different age and circumcision descriptions.

relationship: Same-chapter recovery follows the commanded circumcision
rationale: The people's rest in camp until recovery follows the command, stone-knife preparation and circumcision, linking the stated physical condition with this particular completed action.

relationship: Gilgal's name explanation and the preceding camp notice
rationale: The removal-of-reproach declaration is followed by the naming of Gilgal; the preceding itinerary already identifies Gilgal as the camp east of Jericho, without a modern site identification.

relationship: Passover on the fourteenth day at evening
rationale: Joshua records the Passover on the month's fourteenth day from evening; Exodus' household instruction assigns the Passover slaughter to that fourteenth day toward evening.

relationship: Unleavened food in the Passover setting
rationale: Israel's land-grain meal includes unleavened bread after Passover; Exodus commands unleavened bread for seven days, without requiring Joshua's brief meal notice to narrate all seven days.

relationship: Manna's endpoint at the inhabited Phoenician land
rationale: Joshua records manna ceasing after the land's grain was eaten and a Phoenician-country harvest; Exodus states that manna lasted until the inhabited land and the region of Phoenicia.

relationship: Same-chapter armed figure questioned and his declared role
rationale: Joshua asks the drawn-sword figure which side he belongs to; the following response identifies his claimed role as chief captain of the Lord's host, without an additional personal identification.

relationship: Same-chapter request for instruction and the captain's command
rationale: After the captain announces his arrival, Joshua falls down and asks what his master commands; the next response commands loosening the sandal because the ground is holy.

relationship: Footwear removal at a declared holy place
rationale: Both command removing footwear because the place of standing is holy; Exodus places the command in the burning-bush encounter, while Joshua's speaker is the Lord's chief captain.

relationship: Same-chapter fortified closure contrasted with promised delivery
rationale: Jericho's complete closure and fortification set the immediate scene for the Lord's announcement that He is delivering the city and its king into Joshua's power.

relationship: Same-chapter promised city delivery and narrated capture
rationale: The Lord announces delivery of Jericho; the later account describes the wall falling, the people entering and Joshua putting the city under the ban, without separately inventing a narrated royal death.

relationship: Same-chapter fighting-men stationing developed by procession instructions
rationale: The brief instruction to station fighting men around Jericho is followed by encirclement and ark-procession directions, preserving the actual gap at6:4 rather than supplying another edition's missing instructions.

relationship: Same-chapter cry-and-collapse prediction and reported event
rationale: The instruction predicts a united cry, falling walls and direct entry; the later account records trumpet sound, a united mighty shout, the wall falling and entry.

relationship: Same-chapter approach to priests and the ensuing directions
rationale: Joshua's approach to the priests introduces his specific directions about instructing the people, encirclement, fighting men, seven trumpets and the covenant ark.

relationship: Same-chapter armed advance and specified procession positions
rationale: The command for fighting men to pass armed before the Lord is developed by their going in front and priests behind the ark, preserving the stated roles without inventing an additional group.

relationship: Same-chapter seven priests and seven trumpets repeated
rationale: Both describe seven priests with seven trumpets passing before the Lord and sounding them; the later unit additionally describes the following crowd, whose placement is retained as written.

relationship: Same-chapter front and rear roles develop the preceding orders
rationale: The fighting-men front and priestly rear-guard instruction develops the preceding directions about armed men, seven trumpet priests and the ark; distinct positions are not collapsed into a single priestly group.

relationship: Same-chapter silence-until-command and the later shout order
rationale: Joshua prohibits a cry until it is commanded; on the seventh circuit he expressly commands the shout because the Lord has handed over the city.

relationship: Same-chapter completed circuits followed by camp return
rationale: The ark's return and rest in camp after encircling the city correspond to the later repeated return-to-camp notice across six days, preserving the different stated subjects.

relationship: Same-chapter second-day departure and described procession
rationale: The second-day morning rise and lifting of the ark lead into the seven trumpet priests, following crowd, city circuit and return to camp, without rewriting the day as the first.

relationship: Same-chapter trumpet-priest arrangement follows prior instruction
rationale: The seven priests carry seven trumpets before the Lord, matching the earlier direction for that particular priestly group, without harmonizing every other participant's described position.

relationship: Same-chapter six-day pattern and seventh-day change
rationale: The repeated return after circuits is said to occur for six days; the next unit moves to the seventh day's dawn and explicitly says six circuits before the following seventh-circuit unit.

relationship: Same-chapter sixth circuit notice followed by seventh-circuit signal
rationale: The seventh-day dawn notice says they went around six times; the following unit places trumpet sound and Joshua's shout command on the seventh circuit, retaining both statements.

relationship: Same-chapter announced delivery repeated at the shout command
rationale: Joshua's declaration that the Lord handed over the city repeats the earlier divine assurance of its delivery, now accompanying the prescribed cry rather than an already completed entry.

relationship: Rahab household exception corresponds to the mercy undertaking
rationale: The city's ban expressly excepts Rahab and her house; her earlier request sought mercy and household survival, accompanied by the men's life pledge and her appeal for faithfulness.

relationship: Warning against taking banned property and the following offense
rationale: The warning says taking banned property would endanger Israel's camp; the next chapter reports Israel's misappropriation, names Achar's act and states the Lord's anger against Israel.

relationship: Same-chapter treasury metals instruction and narrated exception
rationale: The instruction assigns silver, gold, bronze and iron to the Lord's treasury; the burning account expressly preserves those metals for that destination while burning the city.

relationship: Jericho's falling walls recalled as a faith example
rationale: Joshua records trumpet sound, united shouting and the wall falling; Hebrews explicitly identifies Jericho's walls falling after seven days of encirclement and gives its faith interpretation.

relationship: The inherited-city ban and Jericho's narrated destruction
rationale: Deuteronomy prescribes destruction in the inherited nations' cities; Joshua describes Jericho and its people and livestock put under the ban, preserving the particular listed victims and agents.

relationship: Ordered rescue of Rahab answers the prior life undertaking
rationale: Joshua orders the same two spies to bring Rahab and her belongings out; their earlier exchange contains her household-rescue request and their life-for-life pledge.

relationship: Named gathered household subsequently brought out
rationale: The rescue names Rahab's father, mother, brothers and all kin, corresponding to the earlier instruction to gather the father, mother, brothers and paternal house together.

relationship: Same-chapter burning account preserves the specified treasury metals
rationale: The city burns except for silver, gold, bronze and iron sent to the Lord's treasury, following the earlier particular assignment of those four metals.

relationship: Rahab's survival and reception of the spies recalled
rationale: Joshua records Rahab and her paternal household surviving because she hid the spies; Hebrews names her survival through faith and peaceful reception, preserving the different stated descriptions.

relationship: Jericho rebuilding account explicitly linked to Joshua's word
rationale: Both connect Jericho's rebuilding with Abiram at the foundation and the younger son at the gates; Kings explicitly cites Joshua's word but names Hiel and Segub, while Joshua names Ozan and an unnamed youngest son.

relationship: Divine presence promised and reported with Joshua
rationale: The account reports the Lord being with Joshua and his name spreading; the opening divine assurance had promised to accompany him as Moses, without equating Israel's and the land's full responses.
